subject: society
topic: Your smartphone's notification sounds are designed to trigger dopamine spikes
angle: While technology companies use psychological cues and alerts to trigger dopamine responses and hijack attention, the evidence focuses more on the resulting cognitive load and habits than on specific variable reward schedules.
title: The Architecture of Attention

hooks.text: Does your phone choose what you see first?
You think you are checking your phone. The design is checking you.
You are letting notifications dictate your focus.
A screen glows in a dark room.

reveal.headline: Your brain releases dopamine when you receive alerts.
reveal.body: Neuroimaging tests confirm that participants experience a dopamine response when they receive alerts. The evidence on how these cues hijack attention is currently emerging and has not been peer-reviewed.

explain.headline: Digital cues are designed to capture your attention.
explain.body: Technology companies use psychological cues to create experiences that capture your focus. These notifications can hijack your attentional resources even when the information is not personally relevant to you.

matters.headline: Your focus is being diverted.
matters.body: The constant stream of notifications may be why you find it difficult to engage in proper interactions or stay focused on your work throughout the day.

example.headline: The steady hum of your phone on a desk.
example.body: You sit down to write a report. A small light flashes or a tone sounds. You look at the screen. You look back at your work, but your focus is gone.

question.headline: Who is deciding what you notice first?

claims.text: Modern digital cues can hijack attentional resources even when they are not personally relevant.
claims.quote: Together, our results show that modern digital cues can hijack attentional resources, even in the absence of explicit personal relevance.

claims.text: Technology companies use psychological cues to design digital experiences that capture people's attention.
claims.quote: Our study showed that technology companies employ psychological cues to design digital experiences that capture individuals' attention.

claims.text: Social media notifications are linked to changes in pupil dilation, which is a physiological marker of cognitive load.
claims.quote: These findings were mirrored in changes in pupil dilation, a physiological marker of cognitive load, confirming the convergent impact of notification relevance and smartphone habits.

verdict: The sources confirm that notifications trigger dopamine and hijack attention, but they do not explicitly link these mechanisms to gambling-style variable reward schedules.
caveat: One source regarding the hijacking of attention is a preprint and has not yet been peer reviewed.
caption: Your phone is designed to capture your attention. Research shows that notifications trigger dopamine responses and can hijack your attentional resources even when they are not relevant to you. Some evidence regarding how these cues hijack attention is currently emerging and has not been peer-reviewed. How much of your day is spent reacting to your device?
